The African Rural and Agricultural Credit Association (AFRACA), in collaboration with NIRSAL Plc and other partners, has brought together financial sector professionals from across Africa in Lagos for a week-long masterclass focused on strengthening agricultural finance through climate resilience and artificial intelligence. The AFRACA Masterclass on Inclusive Finance for Climate Resilience and Artificial Intelligence for Financial Services and Agricultural Finance, which commenced in Lagos on August 19, is attracting participants from Nigeria, Uganda, Ghana, Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Kenya and other African countries. Four central banks are represented at the programme, alongside commercial banks, insurance companies, development finance institutions and microfinance banks. Opening the programme, AFRACA Secretary-General, Ngo Bakang Anny Caroll, expressed satisfaction with the return of the organisation’s capacity-development programme to Nigeria for the first time since 2017. She said the programme was particularly important against the backdrop of climate change and increasing pressure on food systems across Africa. Caroll stressed the responsibility of financial institutions as custodians and allocators of capital to strengthen Africa’s capacity to feed itself sustainably while improving its competitiveness in the global economy. NIRSAL Plc was represented by a delegation, led by its Executive Director, Operations, Ewaen Imohe, who delivered a welcome address on behalf of the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer, Sa’ad Hamidu. Hamidu said the masterclass addressed a major challenge facing agricultural finance in Africa — the relationship between knowledge, risk and financial institutions’ willingness to provide funding to the sector. He said expanding agricultural finance required continuous improvement in the knowledge, systems and capabilities used to source, structure, deploy and manage funds. “At NIRSAL, we have always maintained that agriculture, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, is not underfinanced because opportunities do not exist, but because the risks have not been sufficiently understood, measured, appropriately priced, and managed,” Hamidu said. He said NIRSAL had responded by developing systems and financing frameworks designed to structure agricultural value chains, identify and mitigate risks and improve lenders’ understanding and confidence in the sector. According to him, NIRSAL approved Credit Risk Guarantees for loans exceeding N100 billion in 2025 and had already surpassed that figure in 2026, year-to-date. READ ALSO: FGN bonds make up 96% of government investment for pension funds . He said the guaranteed financing was supporting farmers, processors, aggregators, exporters and other businesses across several agricultural value chains. Hamidu also highlighted the growing participation of non-interest financial institutions, which accounted for more than 50 percent of loans guaranteed by NIRSAL in the first half of 2026. He said the development demonstrated the potential of appropriate risk-sharing frameworks to attract different forms of capital into agriculture. The first major theme of the masterclass, Inclusive Finance for Climate Resilience, focuses on equipping participants with practical tools for assessing climate risks and developing bankable adaptation and mitigation projects. Discussions are covering climate-risk assessment, adaptation and mitigation, climate-rationale development, green-project structuring and access to specialised climate-finance mechanisms. Dr Chris Myungu of the Alliance of Bioversity International & CIAT, a CGIAR partner in the programme, introduced participants to the Africa Adaptation Atlas and CGIAR climate-rationale outputs. title: How Has the Data Discussion Evolved Since the Proliferation of AI?
summary: Attending the Communify Intelligence Experience in London, Leon Saunders Calvert, President and Managing Director, Economist Enterprise spoke to FinextraTV to provide insights into how approaches and perceptions towards data have changed. Saunders Calvert said that the importance of data has not changed, but how it can be used and applied has significantly evolved. He mentions many of the opportunities that have arisen since the growth in AI and how this has dramatically transformed the data discussion, and equally the task of sustaining trust and preventing hallucinations. He emphasised the crucial nature of data within decision making and suggested this should remain the basis for how AI is used and applied.
